title: How the Deep Ocean Makes Its Own Light
paragraphs: The deep ocean is usually described in the language of absence.
It is cold, it is black, the pressure is crushing, and no plant or alga can photosynthesize there.
Most of that holds up.
Below about 1,000 meters, sunlight has been absorbed and scattered away to nothing, and the water stays a few degrees above freezing down to the seafloor.
But the blackness deserves a second look.
The deep sea is not a place without light.
It is a place where nearly all the light is made by the animals living in it.
Sunlit water has a light source every animal shares and no animal controls.
In the deep, light is a possession.
An animal that can make a photon can put it where it wants, when it wants, in the color it wants, and every other animal in range has to interpret it.
Four questions follow: how the light is made, why it keeps being invented, what it is used for, and why the answers took so long to gather.
The chemistry is simple in outline and endlessly varied in detail.
A molecule called a luciferin is the fuel, and an enzyme called a luciferase is the machine.
The luciferase binds the luciferin and adds oxygen to it, producing a strained intermediate that comes apart on its own.
The product lands in an excited electronic state, meaning one of its electrons is briefly held higher than it wants to be.
When that electron falls back down, the energy leaves as a photon.
The payout is taken as light instead of heat.
Because so little energy escapes as heat, bioluminescence is often called cold light, and the phrase is literal.
Some organisms run it as a conventional enzyme, turning over fuel to make a steady glow.
Others use a photoprotein, loaded in advance with its luciferin and its oxygen and held, cocked, until a trigger arrives.
The jellyfish protein aequorin works this way, and its trigger is calcium: when calcium floods in, the stored reaction fires at once and the animal flashes.
That same jellyfish supplies a green fluorescent protein, which absorbs the blue light made beside it and re-emits it as green.
Bioluminescence is not a family trait handed down from one ancient luminous ancestor.
It has been invented independently at least 40 separate times across the tree of life, in bacteria, dinoflagellates, jellyfish, worms, crustaceans, squid, and fish.
The luciferases are not related to one another.
They have been assembled again and again out of whatever enzymes happened to be present.
The luciferins, by contrast, are few.
One of them, coelenterazine, turns up in animals from many unrelated phyla, and in a great many of them it is not made at home.
It is eaten.
Animals take it in with their food and route it to their light organs, so the hard part of evolving light is often not the fuel but the machine that burns it.
Why should the same solution keep arising?
Part of the answer is that the starting materials are ordinary.
Cells are already full of molecules that oxidize readily, and an oxidation leaving its product in an excited state is not exotic chemistry.
It is chemistry that usually wastes the excitation as heat.
Any protein rigid enough to hold that excited state can be co-opted into a crude luciferase, and selection can sharpen a crude one.
Even so, making light is not free.
A flash spends fuel, oxygen, and protein, and for a small animal where meals are sparse, that is expensive.
The trait keeps evolving because in the dark it buys something worth the price.
What it buys depends on the physics of seawater.

Clear water transmits blue and blue-green light far better than red or violet, so a signal near 470 to 490 nanometers travels the farthest, and the great majority of marine bioluminescence falls in that window.
Deep-sea eyes have followed, with visual pigments tuned to the same band and little sensitivity to anything else.
A few fish have exploited the gap.
The stoplight loosejaw makes and sees red light, using a pigment derived from ingested chlorophyll to push its vision into a range its prey cannot detect.
The most widespread use of the light is not a signal at all.
It is camouflage.
In the upper several hundred meters a faint blue haze of sunlight still filters down, and anything swimming in it shows from below as a silhouette.
Counterillumination erases the silhouette.
Rows of light organs along the belly emit light downward at the intensity of the water overhead, so a predator looking up sees uniform dim blue where a body should be.
The organs are small optical instruments, with reflectors behind the light source, lenses in front of it, and filters that adjust the color.
The lie has to be a good one.
Too little light and the silhouette survives.
Too much and the animal becomes a lamp.

Several counterilluminating animals adjust their output as the surrounding light changes, dimming as a cloud crosses the surface or as they sink deeper, and some can match the weaker light of a moonlit night.
The disguise also works in one direction only, because it is aimed down.
Whatever an animal gains from below, its own lights are still a beacon to anything beside it or above it.
Other uses of light are meant to be seen.
The burglar alarm hypothesis describes a defense that works by making the attacker conspicuous.
A dinoflagellate being grazed by a copepod flashes, and the flash does the copepod no harm.
It advertises the copepod to a fish, which eats it.
The grazer is removed by a third party the dinoflagellate never touches.
The same logic is proposed for larger prey: an animal seized in the dark may throw a repeating display that a bigger predator can home in on, so the captor's safest move is to let go.
Further tricks fill out the repertoire.
Some shrimp and squid discharge a luminous cloud instead of ink, leaving a glowing distraction where the animal used to be.
Certain worms and brittle stars shed glowing body parts that flash after they detach.
Some animals smear luminous material onto an attacker, marking it in a way it cannot easily wash off.
Light is also used for hunting and for conversation.
The deep-sea anglerfish dangles an illuminated lure in front of its own mouth, turning the visual advantage of darkness into a trap.
Smaller crustaceans release timed trains of glowing droplets in patterns particular to their species, so a signal readable by the right mate is meaningless to the wrong one.
Many animals do not make their own light at all.
They farm bacteria that do.
The Hawaiian bobtail squid hatches without a single symbiont and recruits its bacteria from the seawater around it within hours.
Ciliated appendages on the developing light organ beat seawater toward a set of pores, mucus traps passing cells, and chemical filters winnow the catch until one species is left inside.
The bacteria then hold their light in reserve until they are crowded.
Each cell releases a small signaling molecule, and only when enough cells are packed together for it to build up do they switch on the genes for luciferase.
This density check is called quorum sensing, and it keeps a drifting bacterium from spending energy to glow alone.
The partnership is maintained rather than merely established.
Each dawn the squid expels about 95 percent of the bacteria in its light organ into the water, and the survivors regrow through the day so that a full population is ready for the following night.
Other partnerships have gone further still.

The bacteria in the lures of some deep-sea anglerfish have lost large stretches of their genomes, including genes they would need in order to live on their own, the signature of a symbiont confined for a very long time with nowhere else to go.
That leaves the fourth question: how much of this is there?
The field spent decades underestimating it for reasons that had nothing to do with the animals.
Early sampling was done with nets, and nets are brutal to the animals most likely to be luminous.
Jellyfish and comb jellies arrive at the surface as shreds, and a shredded animal cannot be scored as luminous.
Animals that survive often exhaust their light after handling and arrive dark.
Submersibles brought a problem of their own, since floodlights bright enough to film by wash out any glow.
The resulting census tilted toward tough-bodied crustaceans and fish.

Once video surveys began counting animals in place under dim red light, the numbers moved sharply: in well-studied stretches of the water column, roughly three quarters of the animals observed proved capable of making light.
Caution is still warranted.
A display recorded once in the dark tells an observer what an animal did, not what it was for, and a plausible story about function is easy to construct and hard to test.
Laboratory work supports the burglar alarm in certain pairings, yet many deep-sea displays have never been watched by anyone who knew which predator was nearby.
Function may also be multiple: a light organ can serve as camouflage on one dive and as a signal on another, and its present use need not be the reason it first appeared.
The claim worth defending is the narrow one, that light is common and is made for reasons, rather than a confident purpose assigned to every flash.
What survives all that hedging is still a reversal of the ordinary picture.
The largest habitat on the planet by volume is not an empty dark space with occasional sparks in it.

It is a place where most of the animals carry their own light, where the same few fuels have been harnessed by unrelated machinery over and over, and where a photon is the common currency of hiding, hunting, warning, and courtship.
The deep sea is dark only in the sense that its light has to be earned.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the photon in a bioluminescent reaction leaves the molecule at the moment when
choices: oxygen is first bound and added by the luciferase enzyme
calcium floods in and reaches the luciferin stored in a photoprotein
a green fluorescent protein absorbs blue light and re-emits it as green light
an electron in the reaction product falls back to its lower energy state
heat generated by the reaction escapes into the surrounding water

proof.quote: When that electron falls back down, the energy leaves as a photon.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 walks the reaction in order: oxygen is added, a strained intermediate comes apart, the product lands in an excited state, and the light leaves when that electron falls back down. The photon is the last step, not the first.
distractorNotes: Oxygen goes in earlier in the sequence, which sets the reaction up rather than releasing the light.
Calcium is the trigger for the photoprotein in paragraph 4, so it starts the stored reaction instead of being the instant light departs.
That is the color shift in paragraph 4, which recolors light that already exists.
Paragraph 3 says the payout is taken as light instead of heat, so escaping heat is not where the photon comes from.

questions.stem: The passage gives which reason that most marine bioluminescence falls in the blue-green range?
choices: Blue-green light carries farther than other colors through clear seawater
Blue-green light is the cheapest color for a luciferase to produce
Blue-green light is invisible to the majority of deep-sea predators
Blue-green light is the color of the sunlight that still reaches 1,000 meters
Blue-green light can be produced without using any oxygen

proof.quote: transmits blue and blue-green light far better than red or violet
travels the farthest

questions.why: Paragraph 7 ties the color straight to the physics of water: blue and blue-green travel far better than red or violet, so signals near 470 to 490 nanometers reach the farthest.
distractorNotes: The passage never ranks colors by what they cost to make; the reason it gives is how far the light travels.
The opposite holds in paragraph 7, where deep-sea eyes are tuned to that same band, which is why one fish using red is remarkable.
Paragraph 1 says sunlight is gone below about 1,000 meters, so there is no sunlight down there to match.
Oxygen is required by the reaction in paragraph 3 no matter what color comes out.

questions.stem: The passage describes the luciferases of different luminous groups as
choices: variations on a single enzyme inherited from one ancient luminous ancestor
proteins that most animals obtain from their food rather than build themselves
unrelated proteins assembled again and again from enzymes already present
identical in structure but different in the kind of fuel they will accept
made only by bacteria and passed to animals through symbiosis

proof.quote: The luciferases are not related to one another.
assembled again and again out of whatever enzymes happened to be present

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says plainly that the luciferases are not related to one another and have been put together repeatedly out of whatever enzymes were on hand. The fuel is what gets shared, not the enzyme.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 opens by rejecting a single luminous ancestor.
Diet supplies coelenterazine, the fuel, in paragraph 5, not the enzyme that burns it.
Not being related to one another is exactly the point, so identical structure is what they lack.
Bacterial partnership is one route among several in paragraphs 13 and 14, not the only source.

questions.stem: Quorum sensing, as the passage presents it, keeps symbiotic bacteria from
choices: being taken up by a host species other than the one they belong in
growing beyond the space that is available inside the light organ
losing the genes they would need in order to live independently
being expelled from the light organ when morning comes
making light when they are too sparse for it to be worth the cost

proof.quote: keeps a drifting bacterium from spending energy to glow alone

questions.why: Paragraph 13 describes a density check: the signaling molecule builds up only when cells are crowded, and only then do the luciferase genes switch on, which spares a lone drifting cell the cost of glowing.
distractorNotes: Host selection is handled earlier in paragraph 13 by the mucus and the chemical filters, not by the density check.
Paragraph 13 links the signal to switching on light genes, not to limiting how many cells there are.
Genome loss belongs to the anglerfish symbionts in paragraph 14 and is not governed by this signal.
The dawn expulsion in paragraph 14 is something the squid does, and the density check does not prevent it.

questions.stem: Each dawn, the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid
choices: vents most of its bacteria into the water and regrows them through the day
takes in an entirely fresh population of bacteria from the surrounding seawater
digests the bacteria it holds and absorbs the nutrients they contain
swaps its bacteria for a second species that is better suited to daylight
shuts its bacteria down by withdrawing the oxygen they need

proof.quote: expels about 95 percent of the bacteria in its light organ
the survivors regrow through the day

questions.why: Paragraph 14 puts a number on it: about 95 percent of the bacteria are expelled each dawn, and the survivors regrow during the day so the organ is full again by night.
distractorNotes: Recruitment from seawater happens once, in the hours after hatching, as paragraph 13 describes.
Paragraph 14 says the bacteria are expelled into the water and says nothing about digesting them.
The winnowing in paragraph 13 leaves essentially one species, and no second species appears anywhere in the passage.
Oxygen withdrawal is never mentioned; the reset described there is a physical expulsion.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, "expensive" most nearly means
choices: commanding a high price in a market
unusually difficult for an animal to obtain
demanding in energy and materials
wasteful of the heat a reaction produces
uncommon among the smallest animals

proof.quote: A flash spends fuel, oxygen, and protein

questions.why: The sentence lists what a flash spends, which is fuel, oxygen, and protein, and then calls that expensive for an animal where meals are sparse. The cost is metabolic, not monetary.
distractorNotes: That is the everyday money sense of the word, and no money is involved anywhere in paragraph 6.
Paragraph 6 calls the starting materials ordinary, so the cost is in spending them, not in getting hold of them.
Paragraph 3 makes the point that this reaction gives up very little heat, so waste heat is not the cost being named.
The sentence is about what one flash costs, not about how many animals have the trait.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 13, "recruits" most nearly means
choices: trains for a specialized task
enlists by force
produces internally from its own tissue
draws in from an outside supply
selects from among its own offspring

proof.quote: recruits its bacteria from the seawater around it
hatches without a single symbiont

questions.why: Paragraph 13 says the squid hatches with no symbionts and gathers its bacteria out of the seawater around it within hours. The word is about taking in cells from outside the body.
distractorNotes: No training happens, since the bacteria already carry the machinery to make light.
Nothing in paragraph 13 suggests force; the squid draws in cells that are already drifting past.
The squid hatches without a single symbiont, so the bacteria cannot come from its own tissue.
The bacteria are free-living cells in the seawater, not the squid's young.

questions.stem: Paragraph 9 most strongly suggests that an animal using counterillumination must also be able to
choices: see the light that its own belly organs produce
sense how bright the water above it is
recognize the species of a predator approaching it
produce red light in addition to blue-green light
stop glowing entirely whenever it is threatened

proof.quote: adjust their output as the surrounding light changes
at the intensity of the water overhead

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says these animals adjust their output as the surrounding light changes, dimming as a cloud passes or as they sink. Matching a background that shifts means the animal has to register what the background is doing.
distractorNotes: The organs aim light downward, away from the animal's own eyes, and the passage never asks it to view its own output.
Paragraph 9 is about matching background light; recognizing a species belongs to the courtship signals in paragraph 12.
Red light is the unusual case of one fish in paragraph 7, not a requirement for this disguise.
Going dark would restore the very silhouette the disguise exists to erase.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from paragraph 15 that counts of luminous animals based on net collections
choices: were reliable for jellyfish but not for fish
were abandoned as soon as submersibles became available
overstated the trait, because handled animals flash repeatedly
matched the later video counts once the badly damaged specimens were set aside
understated how common light is, especially among soft-bodied animals

proof.quote: The field spent decades underestimating it
a shredded animal cannot be scored as luminous
tilted toward tough-bodied crustaceans and fish

questions.why: Paragraph 15 says nets shred the animals most likely to be luminous and that a shredded animal cannot be scored as luminous, which tilted the census toward tough-bodied groups. Those counts had to come in low.
distractorNotes: Jellyfish and comb jellies are precisely what the nets destroy, so those counts are the least trustworthy.
The passage says submersibles brought a problem of their own and gives no timeline for retiring nets.
Repeated handling leaves animals dark, which pushes a count down rather than up.
The numbers moved sharply once video counting began, which is the opposite of a match.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
choices: Light production is chemically simpler than the variety of its biological uses would suggest.
The deep ocean is a hostile place that only a few highly specialized animals have managed to colonize.
Partnership with luminous bacteria is the main way that deep-sea animals obtain the light they use.
Making light is normal in the deep sea, and what is known about it has been shaped by how it was sampled.
Improvements in underwater imaging have overturned most of what biologists once believed about the open ocean.

proof.quote: nearly all the light is made by the animals living in it
for reasons that had nothing to do with the animals
most of the animals carry their own light

questions.why: The passage opens by correcting the picture of a lightless deep sea, works through how light is made, why it keeps appearing, and what it does, then explains in paragraphs 15 and 16 why the count was long too low. Both halves of that answer are the spine of the piece.
distractorNotes: True as far as it goes, and it is one thread in the middle of the passage rather than the point the whole piece builds toward.
The first paragraph rejects exactly this empty-desert picture of the deep sea.
Symbiosis gets two paragraphs among many routes to light and is treated as one arrangement, not the main one.
Video methods revise one number in paragraph 15, and the passage claims nothing that sweeping.

questions.stem: The main purpose of paragraph 15 is to
choices: argue that nets should no longer be used in deep-sea research
explain why the collecting methods, not the animals, produced a low early count
describe the physical damage that deep-sea animals suffer during capture and handling
show that submersibles solved the problems the earlier net surveys had created
introduce the claim that most luminous animals in the ocean are gelatinous

proof.quote: for reasons that had nothing to do with the animals
nets are brutal to the animals most likely to be luminous
Submersibles brought a problem of their own

questions.why: Paragraph 15 asks how much bioluminescence there is and answers that the field undercounted it for reasons that had nothing to do with the animals. Everything in it, the nets, the handling, the floodlights, serves that explanation.
distractorNotes: The paragraph explains what nets distort, but it never calls for retiring them.
The damage is evidence inside the argument rather than the reason the paragraph exists.
The paragraph says submersible floodlights created a problem of their own.
Gelatinous animals appear as an example within the argument, not as the paragraph's claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: An assumption is corrected, four questions are posed and answered, and the conclusions are then qualified.
A single hypothesis is introduced, weighed carefully against two competing explanations, and then rejected on the evidence.
One organism is followed closely from start to finish, and general principles are drawn from it at the end.
A history of deep-sea exploration is traced from the earliest nets through modern video methods.
The uses of light are listed one after another, each one supported by a separate experiment.

proof.quote: But the blackness deserves a second look.
Four questions follow
That leaves the fourth question
Caution is still warranted.

questions.why: Paragraph 1 corrects the picture of a lightless deep sea, paragraph 2 sets out four questions, the body answers them in that order, and paragraph 16 pulls back on how far the answers can be pushed.
distractorNotes: No hypothesis is rejected; the closing paragraphs keep the general claim while limiting the specific ones.
The bobtail squid gets close attention in the middle, but the passage is built around questions rather than around one animal.
Methods come up only near the end, and only to explain why one number was wrong.
The uses are described, but no experiments are reported for any of them.

questions.stem: The author's attitude in paragraph 16 toward explanations of what a particular flash is for is best described as
choices: dismissive of the idea that these displays serve any biological function at all
confident that the purpose of each display has now been worked out
careful, holding the general claim while reserving judgment case by case
frustrated with the researchers who study deep-sea behavior
indifferent to whether such explanations can ever be tested

proof.quote: The claim worth defending is the narrow one
easy to construct and hard to test

questions.why: Paragraph 16 keeps the broad claim that light is common and made for reasons, and it withholds only the confident purpose assigned to any single flash. That is caution, not doubt about the whole subject.
distractorNotes: The paragraph keeps the claim that light is made for reasons; what it resists is naming the reason for every flash.
The paragraph says a plausible story is easy to construct and hard to test, which is the opposite of confidence.
No researcher is criticized; the difficulty belongs to the setting, since displays happen unobserved in the dark.
Testability is precisely what the paragraph cares about.

questions.stem: In paragraph 6, the author treats the repeated independent evolution of light as
choices: a coincidence that remains unexplained
an outcome that ordinary cell chemistry makes unsurprising
evidence that the trait must have a single ancient origin after all
a puzzle that undermines current evolutionary thinking
a rare event that required unusual conditions each time it happened

proof.quote: the starting materials are ordinary
is not exotic chemistry

questions.why: Paragraph 6 answers its own question by pointing to ordinary ingredients: cells are already full of molecules that oxidize readily, and any protein rigid enough to hold the excited state can be pressed into service. The repetition is presented as expected, not mysterious.
distractorNotes: The paragraph offers an explanation rather than leaving the pattern unaccounted for.
Paragraph 5 rules out a single luminous ancestor, and paragraph 6 explains why none is needed.
Nothing is presented as overturning evolutionary thinking; building a trait from available parts is treated as routine.
The paragraph stresses that the starting materials are ordinary, which is the argument against rarity.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements about light organs EXCEPT:
choices: Some contain reflectors, lenses, and filters that shape the light leaving them.
Some are stocked with bacteria instead of making the light themselves.
The output of some can be adjusted as conditions around the animal change.
Some must shed the considerable heat their reaction produces.
Some are aimed downward so that an animal's silhouette disappears.

proof.quote: with reflectors behind the light source, lenses in front of it, and filters
They farm bacteria that do.
adjust their output as the surrounding light changes
because it is aimed down
Because so little energy escapes as heat

questions.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 make the point that almost no energy leaves as heat, which is why the passage calls it cold light. There is no meaningful heat to shed, so that statement is the one the passage does not support.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 lists these optical parts by name.
Paragraphs 13 and 14 describe light organs filled with symbiotic bacteria.
Paragraph 9 describes animals dimming and brightening as the surrounding light shifts.
That is the counterillumination described in paragraph 8.

questions.stem: A reader who wanted to know why the bacteria inside some anglerfish lures could not survive on their own would find that explained in
choices: paragraph 5
paragraph 9
paragraph 11
paragraph 13
paragraph 14

proof.quote: including genes they would need in order to live on their own

questions.why: Paragraph 14 is where the anglerfish symbionts appear, and it says they have lost large stretches of their genomes, including the genes they would need in order to live on their own.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 covers the independent origins of luminous chemistry, not any particular partnership.
Paragraph 9 is about matching the background light while counterilluminating.
Paragraph 11 covers luminous clouds and shed glowing body parts.
Paragraph 13 explains how a squid gathers and screens its bacteria, but the genome loss appears in the paragraph after it.
